extracted.intended_audience: general pop-culture/TV readers and fans of Saturday Night Live
extracted.subtask_short: creating sketches that make cast break
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying features of sketch comedy (illustrated with SNL examples) that cause performers to 'break character' or laugh onstage, and what production choices or character traits tend to produce those moments. Useful for sketch writers, performers, or critics studying why live comedy unravels into genuine laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncanny lookalike guest/cameo that provokes laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A guest host or cameo who resembles a recognizable pop-culture figure (e.g., "a man (guest host Ryan Gosling) who looks eerily similar to Beavis") can unexpectedly disrupt the scene and set performers off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Beavis/Butt-Head bit where lookalike audience members cause Heidi Gardner and others to lose it; surprise cameos that play off audience recognition amplify the chance of cast breaking. Use of a recognizable persona or uncanny resemblance as a beat can create an involuntary reaction from performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical props/gags that escalate into chaos
rubrics_metrics.description: Outrageous or poorly-contained props (e.g., a steak that can be 'sawed through — which ended up in her lap', a motorized scooter, a tiny cell phone, pouring milk into a purse, a golf cart plowing through a sign) create visual absurdity that makes performers crack up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical comedy and props that behave unpredictably or are exaggerated in scale/timing increase the likelihood of onstage laughter. Test prop beats for potential to reveal unexpected visual jokes; consider safety but expect uncontrolled laughter when props 'go too far.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters whose outrageous behavior provokes co-stars
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely out-there characterizations (e.g., Chris Farley's 'deranged motivational speaker' Matt Foley; Ego Nwodim's hostile 'Lisa from Temecula'; Rachel Dratch's Debbie Downer) lead scene partners to struggle to keep a straight face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters with extreme attitudes, unique tics or taboo topics that naturally push other actors' limits. The more specific and outrageous the behavior, the more likely spontaneous reactions will occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation and unscripted line changes to 'shake' performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate surprises from writers or co-creators (e.g., John Mulaney changing lines for Stefon without Bill Hader knowing) disrupt expected beats and can cause performers to laugh and break character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant unscripted elements or last-minute changes as a tactical device to unsettle performers and produce authentic laughter. Use sparingly and with collaborators who can respond in the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of cast members known to incite cracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain performers (e.g., Will Ferrell) have a reputation for 'getting cast members to crack' by using timing, physicality, or improvisational instincts that make others laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting or staging moments that feature a known 'disruptor' can be an intentional tool to create spontaneous laughter. Be mindful that this can derail a scene if too contagious or if straight performers cannot hold it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual awkwardness and over-share as a comedic trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches that feature characters who are 'way too open about their sex life' (e.g., 'The Love-ahs') can prompt giggles from scene partners due to discomfort, awkwardness, or taboo humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push boundaries of intimacy or frankness for comedic effect; actors' natural embarrassment or surprised reactions can fuel breaking. Balance with clear beats so the sketch still lands if someone cracks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan/straight performers enhancing the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Having extras or supporting players who remain serious (the article notes 'all the extras in the scene actually do a masterful job of remaining serious') heightens the contrast when leads break character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately cast or direct some performers to play straight to amplify the comedic fallout when principal actors crack. Strong straight-acting helps preserve the sketch if others break and increases audience amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and exaggerated accents escalating into absurd specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies that exaggerate regional accents and overly specific trivialities (e.g., 'The Californians' with 'exaggerated California accents' and obsessive route details) can snowball into performers laughing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lean into hyper-specific, obsessive parody details to create mounting absurdity; this escalation frequently undermines performers' ability to remain in character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring characters built around breaking tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Some recurring characters (e.g., Stefon) are crafted such that the performer 'often broke,' with physical gestures like covering the mouth or burying the head when they laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating recurring bits, accept and exploit the character's propensity to unspool live — the anticipation of possible breaking can become part of the charm. Plan edits or cutaways when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-show unpredictability and viral potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Moments that cause cast to break (e.g., scenes that 'went viral') are often products of live-TV dynamics and audience reaction, which amplify the humor beyond the broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design bits that can surprise both cast and audience in the moment; the live setting increases the chance that genuine laughter will produce a memorable, talkable clip. Prepare for both rewards (virality) and risks (sketch ruin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketches that survived poor dress rehearsals due to live energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sketches that 'bombed during dress rehearsal' nonetheless worked live because of spontaneous elements that emerged on air (e.g., 'Lisa from Temecula' was 'nearly cut' but succeeded when it 'just kinda started to happen').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't discard material solely based on rehearsal performance—live dynamics and accidental beats can elevate a sketch. Consider keeping risky bits for live shows where unpredictability can pay off.
